planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Temple is a tangor (mandarin-orange cross) that ripens mid-to-late winter and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than true sweet oranges, so it is best sited with wind protection in the cooler parts of its range.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with some wind protection, since Temple is more cold-sensitive than sweet oranges. First found growing in Jamaica and brought into Florida commerce in the early 1900s, it is classed as a tangor, a natural mandarin-orange hybrid, and produces a deep reddish-orange, easy-peeling fruit with an exceptionally rich, aromatic, sweet flavor that many consider superior to either parent type. It ripens January through March, later than most satsumas, giving a late splash of fresh citrus in the garden. Trees are moderately vigorous and benefit from regular citrus fertilizer and consistent moisture during fruit development.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Duncan is seedy but widely regarded as having the richest, most complex flavor of any grapefruit, and the tree is notably cold-hardy for the species.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Traced to a tree found growing on Florida's Gulf Coast in the 1830s and later propagated commercially in 1892 by A. L. Duncan, this is the oldest named grapefruit cultivar still grown today and the ancestor of most modern seedless grapefruit varieties. The pale yellow, white-fleshed fruit is notably seedy by modern standards, but its tart, deeply flavored juice is prized by grapefruit enthusiasts and is still used in breeding programs for flavor quality. The tree is vigorous, productive, and among the more cold-tolerant grapefruit selections, making it a reasonable choice at the cooler edge of the grapefruit-growing range.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Flame is a seedless red grapefruit selected in the Texas Rio Grande Valley and ripens over a long winter window, developing its deepest red flesh color with cool nights.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected and released by Texas A&M's citrus breeding program in 1987 from the Rio Red lineage, Flame produces medium-large, seedless fruit with intensely red-pigmented flesh and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. It is one of the reddest-fleshed grapefruit cultivars commercially grown and holds its color reliably even in warmer winters that can wash out the blush in older red grapefruit types. Fruit matures from late fall through winter and holds well on the tree, allowing a long, flexible harvest window.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Page is a compact hybrid mandarin that ripens in winter and performs well in containers, making it a good choice for gardeners with limited in-ground space.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Developed by USDA researchers in Orlando, Florida in 1963 from a cross of Minneola tangelo and Clementine mandarin, Page produces small, deep reddish-orange fruit with very sweet, richly flavored, easy-peeling segments. The compact, dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be moved to shelter during hard freezes. Fruit ripens from December into February, and the tree benefits from thinning in years of especially heavy fruit set to maintain size.

common_name: Sunburst Tangerine (Deep Orange-Red Florida Hybrid Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Sunburst ripens from November into January and is a heavy, reliable bearer, though fruit should be thinned in on years to avoid excessive limb breakage from heavy crop loads.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1979 from a cross of Robinson and Osceola mandarins, Sunburst produces medium-sized fruit with a strikingly deep orange-red rind and sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh with relatively few seeds. It is one of the more widely planted modern mandarin cultivars in Florida and the Gulf South because of its dependable, heavy annual production and attractive fruit color. The tree bears young and can overbear, so removing some fruit in spring helps maintain fruit size and reduce alternate-year bearing.
